about.title: Clovis Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Clovis families generally trust the clinics, urgent care offices, and hospital departments they rely on across town. Most of the time that trust is well placed. Sometimes, though, a diagnosis is missed, a medication is mixed up, or a surgical step goes wrong, and the person left dealing with the consequences is you. Medical malpractice in California is governed by a specific statute called MICRA, and it sets rules that ordinary injury cases do not have. You usually have one year from the day you discovered the harm to file, and generally no more than three years from the injury itself. Before suing, a 90-day notice must be sent to each provider. Almost every case also needs a qualified medical expert willing to explain how the standard of care was breached. A poor result by itself is not enough. We handle malpractice claims on contingency, so you owe nothing unless there is a recovery.

items.title: MICRA Deadlines Are Unforgiving
items.desc: One year from discovery, three years at the outside, and a 90-day notice before any lawsuit can be filed. Getting started early gives us room to work within those windows.

items.title: Experts Make or Break These Cases
items.desc: California almost always requires a qualified medical expert to testify that the standard of care was violated. We know how to locate and vet the right specialists.

items.title: The Damages Cap Changes Every Year
items.desc: MICRA limits non-economic damages, but that cap rises annually under current law. We can explain how the current figure applies to your situation.

items.question: I saw a doctor in Clovis but was referred to a specialist in Fresno. Where would my case be handled?
items.answer: Clovis and Fresno both sit inside Fresno County, so a lawsuit would ordinarily be filed in Fresno County Superior Court regardless of which office you visited. Each provider involved would need its own 90-day pre-suit notice. We can sort out who bears responsibility and where the claim belongs.

items.question: My surgery didn't turn out the way I hoped. Is that malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law asks whether the provider did something a reasonably careful provider in the same field would not have done, and a disappointing result alone does not answer that question. A qualified medical expert generally has to review your records to say whether the standard of care was breached. That review is one of the first things we would arrange.
